newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek PM's triple win; farmers, seamen, budget.
newsitem.headline: Greek PM's triple win; farmers, seamen, budget.

text.p: Greece's socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis has scored a triple win for his harsh economic reform programme with the adoption of his 1997 budget and the retreat of both protesting farmers and seamen.

The weekend brought Simitis his first major successes since he was elected in September and bolstered his hand in insisting Greece must swallow bitter economic medicine to prepare for a planned single European currency.

"We will take all necessary measures. We will implement all necessary proposals so that Greece responds to the challenge of the European Union," he told parliament shortly before his tough 1997 budget passed early on Sunday.
He vowed "not to bend" in imposing his reforms and bemoaned the fact that Greece came last in almost every EU category.
"Even the Czech Republic and Hungary have better economic indicators than we do," he lamented. "We must go forward as a matter of survival."
Simitis's low-key "no compromise" stand paid off over the weekend when militant farmers called off their 24-day blockade of Greece's main road and rail links.
He had steadfastly refused to give in to their demands and the farmers, after causing weeks of transport chaos and heavy economic damage, came away empty handed.
"We remain committed to our cause and if the government does not act quickly to find a solution we'll be back," said Thanasis Kokinoulis, a member of the radical Thessaly farmers' committee.
Farmers in northern Macedonia and Thrace had lifted their barricades on Saturday, and agreed to meet Simitis on Monday.
With the capitulation of the Thessaly farmers, who started blocking of roads on November 28 and were the most militant, all land transport was again moving freely.
Thousands of Greeks quickly took to the highways, fleeing the cities and returning to their villages for Christmas.
Kokinoulis said the Thessaly farmers lifted their road and rail blockades as a gesture of Christmas goodwill to the public which, he said, had supported the farmers during their protest.
Simitis also received a fillip from seamen who suspended a five-day national strike late on Friday, freeing transport and passenger ships which had been trapped at port.
Like the farmers, the seamen vowed to strike again if the government failed to meet their demands quickly, especially that tax exemptions be reinstated and their pension fund overhauled.
But Simitis has said the state must cut big deficits to meet EU targets. He said farmers were unrealistic in demanding higher price supports, cheaper fuel and rescheduling of $1.3 billion in debts.
The farmers' ragtag army of 10,000 tractors, which had cut off whole regions of Greece, vanished from roads and rails in hours.
Long stretches of national motorways looked like abandoned refugee camps. Public clean-up crews moved in quickly to clear the mess and firetrucks hosed down roads with water cannon.
Miles of debris was left behind by the farmers, who had set up sprawling tent cities which developed into elaborate camps with television sets and generators to light up Christmas trees.
